slides.oldHtml:
Moons

Rocky bodies (mostly spherical) that orbit planets
Formed at the same time as the planets
There are hundreds of moons in the solar system
slides.newHtml:
Moons

Natural satellites that orbit planets
  • Rocky bodies (mostly spherical)
  • Formed at the same time as the planets
  • Hundreds of moons exist in our solar system
Held in almost circular orbits by the planet’s gravitational force

slides.title: Gravity causes orbits
slides.oldHtml:
Gravity causes orbits

The gravitational force between two objects keeps one in orbit around the other
It depends on their masses and the distance between them
slides.newHtml:
Gravity causes orbits

The gravitational force pulls moons around planets, planets and comets around the Sun, and satellites around Earth
Larger masses → stronger gravitational pull
Smaller distance → stronger gravitational pull

slides.title: Elliptical orbits
slides.oldHtml:
Elliptical orbits

Fastest near the Sun
Slowest furthest away
Falling towards the Sun, gravity speeds it up
Moving away, gravity slows it down
slides.newHtml:
Elliptical orbits

Fastest — near the Sun
  • Stronger gravitational pull closer to the Sun
  • Falling inwards, gravity speeds the comet up
Slowest — far from the Sun
  • Weaker gravitational pull far out in space
  • Moving away, gravity pulls back and slows it down

slides.title: Artificial satellites
slides.oldHtml:

High orbits: communication (geostationary)
Low orbits: monitoring the Earth
Polar orbits pass over the whole Earth
slides.newHtml:
Artificial satellites

High (geostationary)
Orbits in 24 hours above one spot — ideal for TV & communication
Low Earth orbit
Close to Earth, fast orbit — monitoring & sharp imaging
Polar orbit
Passes over North & South Poles — scans the whole Earth as it spins

Amount of matter in your body — 100 kg everywhere in the universe

slides.title: Orbital speed
slides.oldHtml:
Orbital speed

v=2πrT
Closer bodies move faster
slides.newHtml:
Orbital speed

v=2πrT
  • r = orbital radius (distance from centre)
  • T = time period (time for one full orbit)
  • Closer bodies feel stronger gravity → move faster

slides.title: Orbital speed: watch the units
slides.oldHtml:
Orbital speed

orbital speed=2 × π × orbital radiustime period
Distance and time must be in the units the answer needs:
m and s → m/s · km and days → km/day
slides.newHtml:
Orbital speed: watch the units

orbital speed=2 × π × orbital radiustime period
Distance in m and time in s → speed in m/s
Distance in km and time in days → speed in km/day

slides.title: Worked example: Mercury
slides.oldHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

Mercury takes 87.97 days to orbit the Sun. Its orbital radius is 57.91 million km. Find its speed.
distance = 2 × π × 57.91 million km = 363.9 million km
speed = 363.9 million ÷ 87.97 = 4.14 million km/day
in m/s: 4 140 000 000 m ÷ 86 400 s = 47 900 m/s
slides.newHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

QUESTION: Mercury takes 87.97 days to orbit the Sun. Orbital radius = 57.91 million km. Find its orbital speed.
Step 1 — One orbit distance (2πr)
2 × π × 57.91 million km = 363.9 million km
Step 2 — Divide by time period (T)
363.9 million ÷ 87.97 = 4.14 million km/day
Step 3 — Convert to m/s (1 day = 86 400 s)
4 140 000 000 m ÷ 86 400 s = 47 900 m/s

slides.title: Learning pit stop
slides.oldHtml:
Learning pit stop

Your turn: use v = 2πr ÷ T. Click to check each answer.
1. A rock on a string is swung round in a circle of radius 1.2 m. One turn takes 0.5 s. Find its orbital speed.
→ 2 × π × 1.2 ÷ 0.5 = 15.1 m/s
2. The Moon orbits the Earth in 27 days. Its orbital radius is 362 600 km. Find its orbital speed.
→ 2 × π × 362 600 ÷ 27 = 84 400 km/day (977 m/s)
3. A woman stands on the equator. The Earth's radius is 6371 km and it turns once in 24 hours. How fast is she moving?
→ 2 × π × 6 371 000 ÷ 86 400 = 463 m/s

slides.title: Geostationary satellites
slides.oldHtml:
Geostationary satellites

Stay above the same point: one orbit every 24 hours
Height 35 000 km, Earth’s radius 6400 km. Speed?
r = 41 400 000 m · T = 86 400 s
v = 2π × 41 400 000 ÷ 86 400 = 3010 m/s
slides.newHtml:
Geostationary satellites

Challenge
A geostationary satellite orbits once every 24 hours at height 35 000 km above Earth’s surface (Earth’s radius = 6400 km). Find its speed in m/s.
Watch the exam trap: r is from Earth’s centre!
  • r = 6400 + 35 000 = 41 400 km = 41 400 000 m
  • T = 24 × 3600 = 86 400 s
v = 2π × 41 400 000 ÷ 86 400 = 3010 m/s

slides.title: How stars are born
slides.oldHtml:
How stars are born

A nebula (cloud of hydrogen gas and dust) collapses over millions of years due to gravity
A protostar forms where it is hot and dense
Hot enough → fusion starts: a star
slides.newHtml:
How stars are born

1. Nebula
Giant cloud of hydrogen gas and dust pulled together by gravity over millions of years
2. Protostar
Collapsing core becomes hot and dense (gravitational potential → thermal energy)
3. Main sequence star
Hot enough in the core → hydrogen fusion ignites: a star is born!

slides.title: Like hot metal
slides.oldHtml:
Like hot metal

Heat metal and it glows red, then orange, then white
The hotter the star, the bluer it is
slides.newHtml:
Like hot metal

Heating metal
Glows red → orange → yellow → white-hot
Same rule for stars
  • Coolest stars glow red
  • Hotter stars glow yellow / white
  • The hottest stars glow blue

slides.title: Main sequence stars
slides.oldHtml:
Main sequence stars

For most of a star’s life it is stable
Gravity pulls the gas in
Heat and pressure from fusion push it out
The two forces are balanced
slides.newHtml:
Main sequence stars

For most of a star’s life, it is stable:
Inward force
Gravity pulls all the gas inwards
Outward force
Heat & radiation pressure from hydrogen fusion push outwards
Inward gravity = Outward pressure → STABLE

slides.title: Red giants
slides.oldHtml:
Red giants

When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the star expands
Much bigger and cooler
Red because it is cooler
slides.newHtml:
Red giants

When core hydrogen runs out, the star leaves the main sequence:
  • The outer layers expand enormously
  • Its surface becomes much cooler
  • Cooler surface → glows red
Later it sheds its outer layers, leaving a tiny, hot white dwarf

slides.title: Supernova
slides.oldHtml:
Supernova

A red supergiant collapses and explodes
About one every 50 years in a galaxy like ours
slides.newHtml:
Supernova

A red supergiant collapses violently and explodes
  • Can outshine an entire galaxy for weeks
  • About one every 50 years in a galaxy like the Milky Way
  • Leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole
Crab Nebula — remnant of a 1054 AD supernova (Hubble)

slides.title: Black holes
slides.oldHtml:
Black holes

All the mass squashed into a tiny point
Past the event horizon not even light can escape
slides.newHtml:
Black holes

Formed by the collapse of the most massive stars
  • All the star’s remaining mass is crushed into a tiny point
  • Gravitational field strength is unimaginably strong
Past the event horizon, not even light can escape!
